topics.topic: Definition, contents, and filesystem accessibility of the sandbox own_proc surface
questions: What exactly is `own_proc`, and must each sandbox expose a private proc filesystem or other process-information surface to agent code?
What exactly is `own_proc`, and may function code open paths in it despite the rule-4 path trap?
What exactly is `own_proc`, and which process information must a function be able to observe through it?

judgement.why: This is the same question about own_proc's definition, contents and accessibility already decided in P3, and the passages at issue have not changed.

precedent.topic: Definition, contents, and function-code accessibility of sandbox own_proc
quotes: execute_function: [SECURITY_BOUNDARY] MUST start bubblewrap with new user, PID, IPC, UTS and network namespaces and no network interface but the new namespace's own loopback, which bubblewrap brings up, with no capability option, the environment cleared and then set exactly to the imported SANDBOX_ENVIRONMENT constant, exactly the host paths of the imported SANDBOX_RUNTIME_PATHS constant bound read-only, inside the new root the symbolic links of the imported SANDBOX_ROOT_SYMLINKS constant (each name linking to its target, made by bubblewrap --symlink), one fresh private exchange directory bound read-write, bubblewrap's own fresh proc mounted at the imported SANDBOX_PROC_MOUNT constant and minimal dev mounts, and no other host directory; the child dies with its parent, and the runner is the init of the new PID namespace (bubblewrap --as-pid-1), so bubblewrap exits only after the host kernel has killed and reaped every other process of that namespace.

The place is now `SANDBOX_PROC_MOUNT` in the data provider
    (`/proc`): `execute_function` mounts the proc there, `runner_arguments`
    passes it as the member `proc_directory`, and the runner lists it.
precedent.why: The later texts require bubblewrap's fresh private proc filesystem to be mounted at `/proc`.

topics.topic: Whether purity forbids all time/randomness sources or only traps the enumerated entry points
questions: Must every standard-library clock or randomness entry point raise, or only the closed A03 list, with unlisted standard-library entry points treated as an undetected way of obtaining time or chance?
Is equal input required to yield equal output for every admitted function, or may an admitted function deliberately use an untrapped time/chance source and vary between executions?

Are functions allowed to produce output dependent on an untrapped source of time or chance, or must the purity/no-clock/no-randomness rule still cause such an execution or implementation to be refused?

judgement.why: This is the same question about untrapped time or chance sources already answered in P2 by the revised K-02 passage, which has not changed.

precedent.topic: Whether executions using untrapped time or chance are permitted or must be refused
quotes:
The standard library's own entry points for the clock and for
randomness raise in a function, so it cannot depend on the time or on chance by
accident; code written to get time or chance some other way is not detected and is
judged by its outputs like any other.
precedent.why: The revised State 0 passage expressly says an untrapped route is not detected and its outputs receive the ordinary validation and outcome treatment.

topics.topic: Whether one-time corpus admission permanently guarantees repaired behavior for nondeterministic implementations
questions: Does passing each corpus case once permanently establish that the implementation stays repaired, or is the guarantee intentionally lost for implementations that obtain time or chance?
Does passing a captured case once permanently satisfy the repaired-slot guarantee, or must the kernel prevent an admitted implementation from later producing an output that fails that same case?

quotes:
Each contract version has a trial corpus; a failed real execution can be captured into it, so a
repaired slot stays repaired.

The standard library's own entry points for the clock and for
randomness raise in a function, so it cannot depend on the time or on chance by
accident; code written to get time or chance some other way is not detected and is
judged by its outputs like any other.
judgement.divergence: One passage requires a captured failure to stay repaired, while the other permits an untrapped time- or chance-dependent implementation to be admitted after one successful corpus execution and later fail on the same captured input; the later run's caller observes the recurrence.
judgement.why: The revised permission for undetected time- or chance-dependent behavior makes the repaired-slot guarantee false under A04's recorded-verdict reuse.

witness.initial: A failed real function execution on input x has been captured as a trial case with no expected outputs, and the replacement implementation uses an untrapped time- or chance-dependent branch that sometimes succeeds and sometimes fails on x.
events: An owner or authoring agent captures the failed execution into the trial corpus.
An authoring agent submits the replacement when its admission execution on x succeeds; the kernel records an admitted verdict and activates it.
An owner or agent later runs the active flow on x in a fresh sandbox when the same implementation's branch fails.
The authoring agent submits the equal implementation again with the unchanged corpus digest, and the kernel reuses the recorded admitted verdict.
outcomes: The repaired-slot passage requires the captured failure not to recur after the replacement is admitted.
The non-detection and admission rules allow the replacement to remain admitted and active even though the later real execution repeats the captured failure.
witness.observer: The owner or agent who started or inspects the later run.
basis:
Each contract version has a trial corpus; a failed real execution can be captured into it, so a
repaired slot stays repaired.

The standard library's own entry points for the clock and for
randomness raise in a function, so it cannot depend on the time or on chance by
accident; code written to get time or chance some other way is not detected and is
judged by its outputs like any other.

Submitting an implementation — new, or equal to an existing one — runs
   admission unless an AdmissionVerdict M08 for that implementation and the
   current corpus digest already exists, in which case that verdict is used.

A case passes when the execution succeeded and, if the case states expected
   outputs, every output's digest equals the expected one — a file output is
   recorded in the TrialExecution by digest, size and media type, keeps no bytes,
   and is compared with the expected file fixture by digest; a `many` file output
   equals its expected list when both have the same length and the digests are
   equal position by position, so order and repetitions count; outputs that
   validate but differ are `output_mismatch`. The verdict is `admitted` exactly
   when the corpus is non-empty and every case passed; otherwise `refused` with
   reason `empty_corpus`, or with the first case in corpus order that did not
   pass and its outcome.

An `admitted` verdict is followed at once, in the same request, by an
   Activation M09 by the kernel — unless that implementation already is the
   current activation, in which case nothing is recorded.
